Entries.SourceTerm: 要會臨濟賓主句，問取堂中二首座

Senses.PreferredTarget: To understand Linji’s guest-and-host saying, ask the two head monks in the hall
SearchAliases: to understand linji’s guest-and-host saying, ask the two head monks in the hall
Senses.Note: Two head monks meet and shout together. Asked whether guest and host remain distinct, Linji says they do, then tells the assembly to ask those two monks. Feiyin asks how anyone can tell which is which without reducing the encounter to a formula. Fushi proposes a strike in place of Linji’s reply. Sanfeng presses both the possibility and impossibility of dividing the roles. Xingkong argues that the monk who raised the question brought the difference to light. The saying sends explanation back to the encounter itself.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J28/J28nB206.xml). Recorded Sayings of Monk Xiaotang. The pair allows going and staying without obstruction, but its local force ranges from funeral farewell to monastic instruction. At the closing of the coffin of his lineage nephew Huolang, Xiaotang strikes the incense table with his staff and refuses to pronounce either 'life' or 'death.' He gives the pair amid lines of freedom from constraint, still mountains, quiet water, clouds returning and an autumn moon setting. He then asks how to state the present sentence, looks to either side and says, 'Close.' The words accompany the actual closing rite; they do not certify a literal journey made by the deceased or biological kinship between the two monks.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J38/J38nB406.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Tianran of Mount Lu. Tianran Hanshi writes the pair in a right-wall inscription. With no inward entangling thought and no surplus external property, the speaker has one bottle, one bowl, one staff and one hat, and may go or stay. The inscription then demands conduct worthy of the ancients and honest toward later descendants, preserving an example for future observance. Senses.Explanation: Silence and speech are available as one chooses, rather than requiring one fixed response. Masters apply this pair within talk of the staff’s full range and of functioning without a prescribed track. Zhe'an Jingfan first sets out a difficulty: silence can sink beyond the ages, while speech can wander in present time. He asks how a monk is to satisfy his life’s intention under that description. Raising the staff, he says that its stillness does not sink on that farther side and its movement does not wander in present time. Only then comes ‘Be silent when you wish; speak when you wish.’ The availability of either follows the stated removal of the two limiting alternatives; it is more specific than a general recommendation to do whatever one likes. Liao'an Qingyu supplies a parallel verbal setting: ‘Great functioning appears before you, without ruts or tracks.’ The pair follows this, then ‘Point to a deer as a horse; call the sun the moon.’ In his address, silence and speech belong to the stated lack of a fixed track. His later mention of Linji and Deshan is part of his appraisal; neither earlier master is the speaker of this occurrence.

Occurrences.Kwic: 入門便棒，是甚機用？趁得老鼠，打破油甕。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X71/X71n1421.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Yu’an Zhiji. Yu'an Zhiji places the pair beneath a heading recalling Deshan striking monks as they enter. His short verse asks what kind of functioning that entrance blow is and answers with rat caught, oil jar broken. The cap tests the action's success together with what it may damage; it cannot be read simply as praise for always striking first. The exact phrase is Yu'an's later verse, while Deshan is the figure whose method is raised. The brief witness does not identify a particular injured monk or narrate a real broken container.

Occurrences.Kwic: 舉僧問大覺和尚。忽來忽去時如何。覺云。風吹柳絮毛毬走。進云。不來不去時如何。覺云。華嶽三峯頭指天。師云。大覺祇解箭鋒相拄。理事相投。殊不知趁得老鼠。打破油甕。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (T/T47/T47n1993.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Huinan of Huanglong. Huanglong Huinan raises a monk asking Dajue about suddenly coming and going, then about neither coming nor going. Dajue answers first with willow fluff blown along, then with Mount Hua's three peaks pointing skyward. Huanglong says Dajue only knows arrow points meeting and principle matching events, without knowing that catching the rat breaks the oil jar. The phrase criticizes an answer that may meet the question yet still incur a loss. The source does not specify that loss as a fixed doctrinal error, so the metaphor should remain an evaluative challenge rather than an invented detailed diagnosis.
